items.ig_caption:
Scripts built to erase data. Every binary backup of its virtual servers, gone. 🗑️

What The Record reported (4 Nov):
→ Russian hosting provider Beget says attackers got into the systems it uses to manage its infrastructure overnight on Sunday 1 Nov
→ They ran scripts designed to erase data. VPS, cloud storage and Kubernetes data was wiped
→ Beget says it lost all binary backups of its virtual servers; file-level backups are intact and may help recover some data
→ More than 1,000 servers must be inspected by hand, so full recovery will take a long time
→ Beget found no evidence attackers downloaded or changed customer data, and hasn't said how they got in. No group has claimed it

The defender's lesson: if one admin system can delete both your servers and your backups, you have one copy. Keep an offline or immutable backup outside its reach, and test restores. Beget also told customers to change passwords and access keys stored on affected systems.

cover.hook: Nvidia's board opens an inquiry: was its CEO a foreign intelligence target?
cover.sub: The board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised.

slides.title: What the board said
slides.body: In a Sunday statement, Nvidia's board said it is starting an independent investigation after reporting that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Independent directors, with outside counsel, will oversee it.

slides.title: The reporting behind it
slides.body: Per CBS, The New York Times reported last month that US authorities were investigating Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.

slides.label: of Nvidia chips bought by Singapore-based Megaspeed in two years, per the NYT (via CBS)
slides.note: One of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia

slides.title: What's not proven
slides.body: Nvidia says Huang fully supports the review. China rejected the allegations last month as "groundless speculation", per the BBC as cited by CBS. No one has shown that any Nvidia data was taken.

slides.title: For your exec protection
items: Brief executives that spies target people, not just networks
Make it easy to report unusual approaches from business contacts
Keep sensitive talks off personal devices and channels
Put relationship-based insider risk in your threat model

items.ig_caption:
A €11.7 billion rail tunnel project. A confirmed data breach. 🚆

What Security Affairs reported (8 Nov):
→ Brenner Base Tunnel (BBT) SE, building the rail tunnel under the Alps, confirms unauthorized people accessed some of its data
→ The Everest extortion group claims 812 GB of files. Nobody has verified that, and ZeroFox notes the group tends to exaggerate
→ The intrusion reportedly dates to mid-October; Austrian press broke the story on 6 Nov
→ BBT SE told ANSA operations are unaffected, the systems involved are isolated, and forensics experts and authorities are investigating
→ No evidence attackers reached industrial systems or tunnel control functions

What to do after a breach like this: find out which information was exposed, revoke credentials that may be compromised, keep document systems apart from industrial networks, and warn suppliers about fraudulent requests.

items.x_text:
Self-hosting an open-weight AI model? Australia's ASD: use approved sources and verify hashes, sandbox first, test for hidden behaviour and prompt injection, put controls between model and systems, and keep a human on risky actions.

#AISecurity #InfoSec
items.ig_caption:
Self-hosting an open-weight AI model? Here's the safe path, step by step. 🧩

Based on new guidance from Australia's ASD (via The Cyber Express, 9 Nov):
→ Risky path: a model file of unclear origin, loaded as-is. Some formats can run code, and backdoors may only show up for certain identities, organisations or topics
→ Then it gets tools and direct access to your systems, with safeguards possibly stripped, raising prompt injection and tool misuse risk
→ ① Get models only from approved, assessed sources and verify hashes and signatures
→ ② Load new models in a sandbox first, and prefer formats that can't contain code
→ ③ Test for hidden behaviours, prompt injection and data leaks before deployment
→ ④ Put external controls between the model and sensitive systems
→ ⑤ Require human approval for high-risk or irreversible actions

ASD's bottom line: if you can't establish where a model came from, don't adopt it. Self-hosting moves security, monitoring and incident response to you, so encrypt and restrict your fine-tuned files too.

Myth: running the AI model yourself makes it safe. Reality: the security job just moved to you. 🤖

What The Cyber Express reported on Australia's ASD guidance (9 Nov):
→ ASD's ACSC published two guides on open-weight AI models, naming examples such as Kimi K3, GLM5.3 and the Nemotron 3 family
→ Unclear origins: you may not know who trained it or on what
→ Tampered files: some formats can execute code, and backdoors may only appear for certain identities, organisations, jurisdictions or topics
→ Fine-tuned files can leak the data you trained them on
→ Safeguards can disappear, raising prompt injection and tool misuse risk in agents

What to do: use approved sources and verify hashes and signatures, sandbox new models first, test for hidden behaviours and prompt injection, and require human approval for high-risk actions. If you can't establish provenance, don't adopt it.
